name: Equine Science & Management

objectives.text: Identify basic external parts of a horse, such as the mane, withers, hoof, fetlock, and muzzle
Identify common horse coat colors and face and leg markings, such as bay, chestnut, blaze, and stocking
Classify common horse breeds as light horses, draft horses, or ponies and describe a typical use for each
Describe the daily care a horse needs, including clean water, forage, grooming, shelter, and hoof cleaning
Explain how a horse shows its mood through ear position, tail movement, and posture and why reading these signals keeps people safe
Demonstrate the correct order and use of basic grooming tools, including the curry comb, body brush, and hoof pick
Identify common items of tack, such as the halter, bridle, bit, and saddle, and explain the purpose of each
Explain how a horse's hindgut digestive system differs from a ruminant's and why horses need frequent small meals of forage
Describe how a horse's height is measured in hands and how its teeth are used to estimate age
Identify plants and feed conditions that are dangerous to horses, such as red maple, yew, and moldy hay
Demonstrate proper haltering, leading, and tying techniques for safely handling a horse
Measure a horse's temperature, pulse, and respiration and compare the results with normal ranges
Summarize the major segments of the equine industry, including breeding, racing, showing, recreation, and working ranch horses
Identify methods used to identify and track horses, such as markings records, brands, microchips, registration papers, and Coggins test documents
Recognize signs of common equine health problems, such as colic, laminitis, and lameness, and explain when to call a veterinarian
Assign a body condition score to a horse using the Henneke scale and explain what the score means for its management
Apply information from a feed label and feeding directions to calculate daily hay and concentrate amounts for a horse
Explain the structure of the equine hoof and the purposes of regular trimming and shoeing by a farrier
Evaluate a horse's conformation and gait using correct equine terminology to judge its soundness and suitability for a particular discipline
Analyze low-stress handling and restraint methods for horses, such as stocks and twitches, for their effect on safety and stress
Explain the mare's estrous cycle, breeding methods such as live cover and artificial insemination, gestation length, and stages of foaling
Develop a balanced ration for a horse based on its work level, growth stage, or gestation and lactation needs
Design a preventive health program for horses that includes vaccinations, deworming guided by fecal egg counts, dental floating, and farrier visits
Evaluate a mare or stallion for breeding readiness and soundness using reproductive history, conformation, and veterinary exam results
Evaluate a stable facility's stalls, fencing, footing, and ventilation for horse safety and welfare
Evaluate equine welfare issues, such as soring, unwanted horses, and long-distance transport, and the programs designed to address them
Recommend treatment and rehabilitation options for common equine conditions, such as colic or laminitis, based on veterinary guidance
Create a management plan and budget for a boarding or training stable that schedules feeding, health care, and farrier work and keeps records suitable for an SAE

changes: Split the grade 2 objective into horse parts (grade 2) and breed classification (grade 4), and added coat colors and markings. Kept and refined daily care, digestive comparison, haltering and leading, and conformation and gait evaluation, and aligned conformation to AS.06.01.03.b. Reframed the grade 12 stable objective as creating a management plan and budget with SAE records. Added missing equine competencies: body language and safety, grooming tools, tack, aging by teeth and measuring in hands, toxic plants, vital signs, industry segments, identification and tracking, recognizing health problems, Henneke body condition scoring, feed label use, hoof care and farriery, low-stress restraint, reproduction, ration balancing, preventive health programs, breeding soundness, facility evaluation, welfare issues, and treatment recommendations. Standards were applied only to grade 9 to 12 objectives where they truly fit.
